metadata_extension.subtitle: China’s reported current account surplus understates China’s contribution to global trade imbalances. The massive gap between China’s export and import volume growth over the last six years tells a more accurate story.

summary.central_question: Why does the IMF fail to see China's huge surplus clearly, and what does that blind spot cost its policy advice?
summary.main_thesis: China's surplus is massive and is the central global imbalance; by relying on understated current account data, the IMF misses it and gives wrong advice and a misdirected global focus.

content.text: Why does the IMF fail to see China's huge surplus clearly, and what does that blind spot cost its policy advice?
content.reason: When the evidence is overwhelming but an official assessment misses it, the measuring instrument deserves scrutiny.

passages.source_excerpt: Yet even with overwhelming evidence of a massive surge in China's exports over the past five years (absolutely, and relative to imports), the IMF has struggled to clearly identify China's outsized contribution to global imbalances.

content.text: China's car exports exceed 6 million and are heading toward 8 million, with BYD aiming at 5 million, and China dominates clean-tech exports.
content.reason: Physical export volumes in key sectors reveal the scale of a trade surplus.

passages.source_excerpt: China's exports of cars has surged to well over 6 million cars (or about a tenth of the global auto market outside of China), and are on a trajectory that will lead to 8 million passenger car exports in 2026.

content.text: In the IMF's own data, export volumes are up 40 percent since 2019 against 1 percent for imports, which implies net exports added over a point a year to growth.
content.reason: A widening gap between export and import volumes shows growth driven by net exports.

passages.source_excerpt: China's exports are up a cumulative 40 percent in volume terms since the end of 2019, while imports in volume terms are up only 1 percent.

reasons: passages: `E2`: the team's passage linker anchors it to p9 (shared: 1percent), which the box does not cite

content.text: Customs data show a manufactured-goods surplus above $2 trillion (10.5 percent of GDP, over 2 percent of world GDP) and an overall goods surplus of $1.2 trillion.
content.reason: A surplus measured against world GDP and historical peaks shows its systemic weight.

passages.source_excerpt: China's surplus in all goods is now $1.2 trillion in China's customs data, after a roughly $800 billion increase over the last 5 year.

content.text: CPB data show China's export volumes outpacing global trade while Europe's shrink.
content.reason: An independent trade-volume dataset can corroborate shifts in market share.

passages.source_excerpt: The Dutch CPB data set on export volumes shows China's export volume growth lapping global trade—as China is rapidly taking market share from Europe.

content.text: Customs trade data and observed physical flows measure China's real imbalance better than its reported balance of payments.
content.reason: Directly observable trade flows are more reliable than heavily adjusted aggregate statistics.

passages.source_excerpt: at least not in the well-measured trade data

content.text: Large global imbalances have returned, and China's growth on the back of net exports points to wider imbalances and more trade tension.
content.reason: A large surplus country growing through net exports pushes global imbalances wider.

passages.source_excerpt: There consequently should be no doubt that global payments imbalances have returned, and are now quite large.

content.text: Weak domestic demand frees capacity for export, and the resulting rate cuts, low yields and a weak, intervention-held yuan push the surplus up further.
content.reason: A demand shortfall leads to monetary easing and currency weakness, which shifts output toward exports.

passages.source_excerpt: The ECB says this ultimately stems from a shortfall in China's domestic demand, which makes sense.

content.text: France wants imbalances to be central at the G-7, and Germany has reasons to agree because of the damage to its industrial base.
content.reason: Governments whose industries are hurt by a partner's surplus push for multilateral attention.

passages.source_excerpt: The French have recognized the risk that China's ever-growing surplus poses to Europe -- and want to make imbalances a central focus of the next G-7 summit.

content.text: The IMF judges imbalances solely on reported current accounts, and China's reported surplus of 2.2 percent of GDP sits only slightly above its estimated norm.
content.reason: The choice of metric decides which imbalances an assessment can see.

passages.source_excerpt: That is IMF relies exclusively on countries' reported current account surpluses and deficits in its assessment of the size of external payments imbalances.

content.text: On the current account measure, Japan, Korea, Germany and even the EU show larger surpluses than China as a share of GDP.
content.reason: When two measures of one imbalance rank countries in opposite order, the gap needs explaining.

passages.source_excerpt: Even the EU's surplus in 2024 was bigger as a share of GDP: 2.6 percentage points of GDP versus 2.2 percentage points of GDP.

content.text: A methodology change cut the measured goods surplus, and an implausible income deficit despite nearly $4 trillion in net foreign assets cuts more, so the reported current account is artificially deflated.
content.reason: A creditor country should earn net investment income, so a reported income deficit signals mismeasurement.

passages.source_excerpt: its 2022 balance of payments methodology magically cut the goods surplus by over a percentage point of GDP, and the mysterious income deficit (in the face of a close to $4 trillion positive net international investment position) knocks another percentage points off the surplus

content.text: Chinese official data cannot be verified: there is no detailed quarterly GDP data and no export volume series.
content.reason: Statistics that no one can replicate deserve less trust than observable physical flows.

passages.source_excerpt: sometimes it pays to watch the flow of container ships and auto transport ships—and not to just trust the Chinese data.

content.text: The IMF forecast China's 2025 surplus to fall to $375 billion, yet it will top $650 billion through Q3 alone.
content.reason: A forecaster that repeatedly predicts a reversal that never comes is likely missing a structural driver.

passages.source_excerpt: The IMF's current account forecasts for China have consistently been off, in part because they treated the surge in the surplus during the pandemic as transitionary

content.text: A property slump and a weaker currency should raise the surplus with a lag, so IMF forecasts of a shrinking surplus contradict the IMF's own logic.
content.reason: Currency depreciation and domestic housing slumps raise external surpluses with a lag.

passages.source_excerpt: because China's property downturn has continued

content.text: Because the surplus looks small, the IMF treats China's problem as purely internal and ignores its external imbalance.
content.reason: A problem that is mismeasured gets misdiagnosed, and the policy advice follows the diagnosis.

passages.source_excerpt: it has allowed the IMF to define China's problem as one of lack of internal balance (deflation, weak employment growth) and not as a combination of a lack of internal balance and a simultaneous lack of external balance.

content.text: The IMF's advice of monetary easing would weaken the yuan and widen the surplus, in effect having China export its way out of its housing slump.
content.reason: A cure that worsens an imbalance the adviser claims to care about is self-defeating.

passages.source_excerpt: The IMF's preferred solution to deflationary pressures in Asia, China included, is generally monetary easing—which tends to weaken the currency and raise the external surplus.

content.text: The IMF should call for a sustained, centrally funded fiscal expansion, including a deficit-financed social safety net, to lift Chinese demand.
content.reason: Deflation together with a rising surplus calls for fiscal rather than monetary stimulus.

passages.source_excerpt: The right response to a shortfall in demand that is leading to deflation and a rising trade surplus, though, is a sustained fiscal expansion

content.text: China's central government has the fiscal space to finance a large expansion without risk.
content.reason: A low-debt sovereign can borrow to support demand without triggering a fiscal crisis.

content.text: The IMF does back bank recapitalization to finish sold apartments and pro-consumption structural reforms, so its advice is not wholly misguided.
content.reason: Give an institution credit for the parts of its advice that point in the right direction.

passages.source_excerpt: to be fair, the IMF does want pro-consumption structural reforms, it just bulks at calling for a bigger structural fiscal deficit

content.text: Others argue that Europe's surplus is nearly as large as China's, so singling out China is not warranted.
content.reason: An aggregate comparison can mislead if one member's figures are distorted.

passages.source_excerpt: I don't know how many times I have heard that Europe's surplus is almost as big and thus a focus on China isn't really warranted.

content.text: Ireland's tax-driven surplus inflates the euro area's surplus, and offshore U.S. profits booked there (Microsoft alone over $40 billion) hide Europe's income balance; net of Ireland, Europe's goods surplus disappears.
content.reason: Profit-shifting by multinationals distorts the trade and income accounts of the host country.

passages.source_excerpt: Its 15 percent of GDP current account surplus adds about half a point to the euro area's aggregate surplus.

content.text: China's surplus is massive and is the central global imbalance; by relying on understated current account data, the IMF misses it and gives wrong advice and a misdirected global focus.
content.reason: Policy institutions should judge imbalances by reliable flow data rather than by distorted aggregates.

passages.source_excerpt: But the result of these statistical shenanigans is rather problematic if it keeps the IMF (and others) from recognizing how much of an issue China's current growth model is for the rest of the world.
